notes.b: Not every food business is a large factory. Small food businesses produce in small quantities, often family-run and rural, for local or niche (specialised) markets, and a home enterprise is the smallest kind.
points: A small business produces in small quantities and sells locally or to a niche market, which is why it is often family-run and based in a rural area.

A home enterprise (also called a cottage industry) is a small food business started and run from a domestic kitchen or a small unit near the home, for example making jams, chutneys, baking, chocolate or honey.

An artisan producer makes food in limited quantities by traditional, non-industrial skills and hand methods, such as hand-baked bread, farmhouse cheese or chutneys. Cashel Blue (Co. Tipperary) and Gubbeen (Co. Cork) are Irish farmhouse cheeses.

Speciality foods are produced in small quantities for a particular market by small businesses or home enterprises, often with local ingredients, little or no additives and a traditional or natural image. Examples include cheese, chutney, jam, honey, bread, home baking, smoked fish, chocolate, yoghurt and ice cream.
Speciality foods also include foods made for special diets, such as gluten-free (for coeliacs), vegan or diabetic foods, and organic foods.
Artisan describes how a food is made (by hand, using traditional skills), while speciality describes the product and its market. The two overlap, and neither is a legally protected term.
Small producers often sell through farmers' markets, food fairs, local shops, restaurants and online, and direct to customers.
Many small producers start from a home kitchen and move to a dedicated unit as demand and production grow.
notes.tip: If asked what speciality foods are, give small quantities, a small business or home enterprise, local ingredients, little or no additives and special diets, then two named examples. Do not claim speciality foods are automatically healthier or organic; say they are perceived as healthier.

notes.h: Role of small producers in the food industry
notes.b: The role of small producers is what they contribute to the food industry and to the country. Each contribution below is a separate point you can develop.
points: They create employment, often in rural areas where other jobs are limited, which helps keep rural communities alive.
They build a skilled workforce, because staff in small firms often handle every stage of production and so learn every stage.
They diversify the industry by making products that large manufacturers do not produce, and they bring out new exclusive ranges as markets change.
They identify and enter old and new niche markets, meeting consumer demand for local, natural, traditional or special-diet foods.
They use locally produced ingredients, which supports local farmers and suppliers and reduces food miles (the distance food travels from producer to consumer).
They promote quality ingredients and innovation, and work to very high standards of hygiene.
They strengthen Ireland's reputation for high-quality food and drink, and promote the region they are based in.
They support rural communities and farm diversification (farmers earning extra income by making food products rather than selling raw produce only).
notes.tip: When asked to discuss or evaluate the role of artisan producers or small businesses, aim for four or five points and develop each in a sentence, point plus reason, rather than listing. Do not mix this with why consumers buy the foods; that is a different question with different marking points.

notes.h: Why small-business foods are growing in popularity
notes.b: Why consumers buy speciality foods is a different question from what small producers contribute to the industry. Features that attract consumers, such as variety, few additives and hand-made quality, are things mass-produced food does not give them.
points: Consumers want greater product variety and flavour than mass-produced food offers, with recipes that large manufacturers do not make.
There is little or no use of additives, so the foods are seen as natural, less processed or healthier. This is a perception, not a guarantee.
Foods are hand-made with close attention to each batch, using traditional skills, which gives them a quality, premium image and a natural, traditional look.
Many consumers are interested in provenance (where food comes from) and traceability, such as knowing the named farm or maker and the Irish origin of the ingredients.
Consumers want to support local producers and jobs, and sustainability through fewer food miles and organic or sustainable methods, including support for local goods in a recession.
There are more routes to market: farmers' markets, food festivals and food tourism, specialist shops, restaurants, supermarkets that stock local lines, online selling, media coverage and food awards.
There is growing demand for special-diet foods (coeliac, vegan, diabetic), which small producers can supply in small runs.
Changing food culture, through travel and multicultural eating, has increased interest in different and unusual foods.
notes.tip: For a question on the growing popularity of speciality foods, give consumer reasons: variety, additive-free, hand-made, natural image, quality, local produce, farmers' markets, supermarkets and online, support for local goods and reduced food miles. Farmhouse cheese works well as a single named example. Do not repeat the same point you used for role.

notes.h: Supports and growth of small Irish producers
notes.b: Small producers rarely start big. They grow step by step, helped by consumer demand and by public bodies that give training and advice.
points: Rising consumer demand for local, speciality and traditional foods has encouraged new small producers to start.
Farmers' markets and food festivals give small producers a direct route to customers without a large distributor, so they can test products cheaply.

Local Enterprise Offices (LEOs), a network of offices run through the local authorities (31 teams), give start-up and development supports to small businesses: training, business courses, mentoring, advice and networking.
Food supports include the Food Starter Programme for people at the idea stage, and the Food Academy, which gives training and mentoring to new food companies and is run with Bord Bia.
Bord Bia and Enterprise Ireland give food companies, including smaller firms, market development and export advice.
The typical growth path is to start at a farmers' market or from the kitchen, move to local shops, then to supermarkets or export, and move from the home kitchen to a registered unit as demand grows.
notes.tip: Questions on why production in small businesses is increasing can ask for two reasons, with a second part on exports. Give demand and the routes to market, and name a support such as the LEOs or Bord Bia.

notes.h: Food safety and regulation for small businesses
notes.b: Making food at home or on a small scale does not lessen the need for safety. A small producer must follow the same food law as a large company, though the paperwork can be scaled to the business.
points: A new food business, including one run from home, must register with the competent authority (the official body in charge) before it starts trading.
For most businesses, such as bakers, caterers and jam and chutney makers, the competent authority is the HSE Environmental Health Service, which inspects the premises for food safety and hygiene.

The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine registers premises handling foods of animal origin such as meat, dairy and eggs. Seafood premises are registered with the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority.

EU food hygiene law, Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, is given effect in Ireland by the European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006. It requires every food business to operate a food safety management system based on HACCP principles.

HACCP identifies the points in production where food safety hazards could occur and sets controls for each one. For a small producer the system can be simple and proportionate to the size and nature of the business, so the standards are the same but the paperwork is scaled.
Prepackaged food must carry the information required by Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.

The required label details are the name of the food, ingredients with allergens emphasised, the business's name and address, date marking and storage instructions. Small firms follow the same labelling rules.
Traceability means producers must know their suppliers and customers, one step back and one step forward (Regulation (EC) No 178/2002), so that a problem food can be traced and recalled.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) provides guidance, including a guide to food law for artisan and small food producers, and food safety training to small food businesses.
notes.tip: Remember that food businesses are registered with the competent authority (HSE, the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, or for seafood the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority), not licensed by the FSAI. The FSAI gives guidance.

keyTerms.definition: A small producer who makes food by traditional or hand methods rather than in mass production.
A food made in small quantities for a particular market, such as organic, gluten-free or vegan consumers.
A small food business started and run from a domestic kitchen or a small unit near the home.
A small, specific group of consumers with particular needs or preferences that a producer targets.
A local market where producers sell their own products directly to customers.
The place of origin of a food and the producer or farm it came from.
A documented set of procedures a food business uses to identify and control food safety hazards.

factCards.term: Four roles of small food producers
factCards.definition: Creating employment, often in rural areas; diversifying the industry with new products; entering niche markets; using locally produced ingredients.

factCards.term: Three features that make speciality foods attractive to consumers
factCards.definition: Little or no additives; hand-made production; a traceable local or named origin.

factCards.term: Three special diets catered for by speciality foods
Two forms of support from Local Enterprise Offices
factCards.definition: Training and business courses; start-up and development advice.

factCards.definition: Register with the HSE Environmental Health Service; operate a food safety management system based on HACCP; meet food labelling and hygiene standards.

questions.prompt: Explain two ways in which small food producers contribute to the Irish food industry.
questions.model: Any two, each explained: employment, often in rural areas, and skilled staff; diversifying the market with artisan or speciality products; using locally produced ingredients that support local farmers and suppliers; meeting niche consumer demand for quality, additive-free or special-diet foods. One mark for each point named and one for each explanation.

questions.prompt: Discuss the role of small businesses and home enterprises within the Irish food industry, referring to speciality foods, the consumer demand behind them and the food safety rules they must follow.
questions.model: Role: create employment, often in rural areas, and build a skilled workforce; diversify the industry and enter old and new niche markets; use local ingredients; promote quality and innovation and strengthen Ireland's reputation for high-quality food and drink. Speciality foods: artisan or hand-made products made in small quantities; little or no additives; variety not offered by large manufacturers; traceable origin; catering for coeliac, vegan and diabetic diets. Demand: consumers seeking local, natural and traditional foods; farmers' markets and food festivals as routes to market; support from Local Enterprise Offices, Bord Bia and Enterprise Ireland. Regulation: registration with the HSE Environmental Health Service, inspection, a HACCP-based food safety management system, the same labelling and hygiene standards as large firms, and FSAI guidance.
